newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Cafe serves up Christian conversion.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cafe serves up Christian conversion.

text.p: The sign outside the door reads "Coffee Shop," but visitors at the cafe just inside Jerusalem's walled Old City get more than a cappuccino.
They get a lesson in Jesus before they leave.

Known in Christian circles as a cafe on the "cutting edge of modern-day evangelism," and to Jews and Moslems as a place to avoid, the Loaves & Fishes Cafe employs young missionaries zealous about spreading the word.
"I want everyone to know the same Jesus I know," said 20-year-old missionary Vicki Gascho of Columbus, Ohio.

"I don't consider myself a real outgoing person. I'd rather stay in the kitchen and wash dishes and let everyone else evangelise. But as hard as it is for me, I'm willing to take rejection if I think it might stimulate someone's heart."

Inside the cafe, where Bible verses and stickers proclaiming "Jesus is Christ" adorn the walls, the 10 volunteers use different techniques to win people over. They play Christian music, hand out Christian literature and start conversations with the customers in the hope of winning over that rare convert.
CONVERSIONS RARE IN EVANGELICAL CAFE
None of the cafe's young missionaries, in the Holy Land only for a short time, has ever engineered a conversion of anyone inside the cafe.
But manager Denis Yancy said it has happened. A Thai woman, living in Israel and married to an Israeli, "came to faith" a couple years ago after several intense conversations over coffee about God.
"One of these days there's going to be a lot of salvation here. But it's not now," said Yancy, of Redondo Beach, California.
In a place where a homesick American tourist can get a non-kosher meal of meat and cheese lasagna, it's hard to get Jews and Moslems to come in, he said.
At lunchtime recently, the cafe was packed -- with Christians only.
"A lot of the volunteers would really like it if the coffee shop was kosher and took down some of the things that scream Christian," said missionary Jason Underwood, 25, of Salem, Virginia.

"From what I understand, the Jewish people are still waiting on the Messiah to come. They missed Jesus," he said. "I came and that really challenged me. You're wondering why they don't see it. What's stopping them. The biggest thing I found is Jesus is taught right out of the prophecies."
MISSIONARIES DON'T FEEL WELCOME IN ISRAEL
No one knows exactly how many missionaries there are in Israel. The Ministry of Religious Affairs does not record the numbers, and the evangelists themselves don't always know who else is out there.
But in a contested city holy to three major faiths, Christian missionaries don't often find themselves well-liked by the other two.
The tense world of Middle East politics, where selling land to the wrong person can get you killed, is foreign to them.
"I think they should all get saved and quit worrying about the land," Underwood said. "I don't think God promised it to me."

Israeli law prohibits missionaries from giving money to persuade people to convert -- those who do could spend five years in jail. But the law is not enforced, a Religious Affairs Ministry official said.
Religious Jewish groups are trying to get parliament to pass a law banning missionaries from distributing literature and introducing a year-long jail sentence to those who do.
Some Moslem clerics have said sharia, or Islamic law, proscribes death for those who leave the faith, and converts in nearby Arab states have reported harassment.
ANTI-MISSIONARY BILL UNLIKELY TO BECOME LAW
Palestinians in Israel's parliament (Knesset) have opposed the anti-missionary law, saying it could hurt the small Palestinian Christian population.
"Every man has a right to speak. That's something that should be legal in Israel," said Abdul-Malik Dehamshe, a member of the Islamic Movement who represents the Democratic Arab Party in parliament.
Although the bill passed a preliminary reading in the Knesset, experts say it is unlikely to become law.

"What we would like to see is respect -- not to have an invasion of our lives," said Judy Zeezi, Head of Archives at Yad L'achim, an ultra-Orthodox group that monitors evangelism and is pushing for the law.
She said she resents the techniques missionaries use and wishes they would just go away.
"They're very nice about it. They don't want us to go to hell. But if we choose to, leave us alone," Zeezi said.
Kudi Adeniyi, from the English resort of Brighton, said 10 years of off-and-on missionary work in the Holy Land have made her realise the risks and frustrations of her profession.
Last year, she said, she finally managed to convert someone.
"I met somebody in a hostel, and after talking about the Lord and asking many questions, he became a believer," she said.
But then she paused and looked around. She debated aloud whether she should reveal the man's original religion and decided against it.
"I don't want to say anything," she said. "You've got to be careful here."
